title: What all share: ethics and practice
hookLine: precepts, meditation and kindness run through every school

cards: Three robes at one breakfast table. Saffron, from a forest monastery in Thailand. Black, from a Zen temple in Japan.
Maroon, from a Tibetan nunnery. One chanted the precepts in Pali before dawn. One sat facing a white wall until the bell.
One recited verses wishing every being well. Three very different mornings.
Listen a little longer, though, and three threads run through all of them: a promise about how to act, a time for training the mind, and a wish for other people's good.

teach.h: SILA: PRECEPTS TAKEN ON, NOT IMPOSED.
teach.b: First, conduct. The Pali word is sila. For lay Buddhists it takes the shape of the five precepts: no killing, no stealing, no sexual misconduct, no false speech, and no intoxicants that cloud the mind.
They aren't commandments handed down but training rules a person takes on: I undertake to train in this.
Monks and nuns keep far more rules, and some Mahayana communities add bodhisattva precepts on top. But the five are the ground floor. Second, training the mind.
Here the schools look very different. Noting the rise and fall of the belly in Burma. Zazen in Japan.
Visualizing a Buddha in Tibet. Walking slowly in a Korean courtyard. Chanting a name in a Chinese hall.
Underneath runs the same work: steadying attention so it can see clearly. Third, kindness. Theravada homes chant the discourse on loving-kindness, metta.
Mahayana temples speak of great compassion, the wish to free all beings. Different words, both wishes for other people's good. Fourth, one verse gathers it all.

teach.h: NOT TO HARM, TO DO GOOD, TO PURIFY.
teach.b: The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, says: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened."
A Thai monk, a Japanese priest and a Tibetan nun could each recite their own version of that line, and mean it.

how: Lay Buddhists in Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana communities often recite the five precepts as training rules they take on, alongside meditation and chanting for the good of all beings.

games.why: the forms differ a great deal, but the same threads run through all three: conduct, meditation and compassion.

practice: Look at the five precepts: not harming, not taking what isn't given, care in desire, honest speech, a clear mind. Choose the one that would stretch you, and hold it in the old formula's plain words: I undertake to train in this.
Then rest with your breath, the promise sitting quietly beside it.

wordCard.voice: What all share. Beneath the robes and the languages: precepts, a trained mind and kindness, running underneath the schools we've met this year. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali sila (Sanskrit shila): conduct, the moral training kept through the precepts.
